einzeiler: Why medical research has treated women as small men and how to fix it
kurzfassung: Katie Couric and Dr. Sharon Malone discuss systemic gender disparities in medical research and healthcare. They examine historical roots from ancient philosophers to modern clinical trials, focusing on the impacts of the Women's Health Initiative. Additionally, they explore how the documentary Hormonal aims to spark a movement for better women's health education and funding.
stichpunkte: Historical medical views often regarded women as inferior or incomplete versions of men.
Female health conditions and Alzheimer's research receive disproportionately low funding compared to male-centric equivalents.
Clinical trials historically excluded women primarily due to complex hormonal fluctuations.
The 2002 Women's Health Initiative study caused widespread panic and halted decades of hormone replacement therapy research.
Flawed study designs and media overreactions led doctors to universally misapply hormone therapy risks.
Conditions like endometriosis face severe diagnostic delays, taking an average of a decade to identify.
Social media is currently filling a massive information vacuum left by the medical establishment's neglect of female health.
The new documentary project seeks to create a lasting social impact campaign similar to successful youth advocacy models.

clips.hook: Erectile dysfunction gets five times the funding of PMS
clips.text: The speakers highlight stark funding inequalities between male-specific conditions and female health issues like Alzheimer's and general R&D.

clips.hook: Over 70 percent of women stopped hormone therapy overnight
clips.text: Media headlines regarding breast cancer risks caused a massive, sudden panic that made millions abandon hormone replacement therapy.

clips.hook: It takes an average of ten years to diagnose endometriosis
clips.text: A staggering delay plagues patients suffering from a common reproductive condition before they receive proper medical answers.

clips.hook: The actual normal amount of blood for an entire period
clips.text: Medical guidance reveals that a healthy menstrual cycle involves a surprisingly small total volume of fluid.

clips.hook: Grading the American healthcare system on women's health
clips.text: Future initiatives involve creating comprehensive indices and mandatory medical school curricula to properly address female medicine.

beschreibung: Katie sits down with Dr. Sharon Malone at the Aspen Institute to talk about why women's health has been under-researched and under-funded for centuries -- which also happens to be the subject of Katie's new documentary, HORMONAL!. The numbers are staggering: PMS affects 90% of women but gets a fraction of the funding erectile dysfunction research receives. The NIH didn't require women to be included in clinical trials until 1993. Katie also shares how her own breast cancer diagnosis has shaped her relationship to hormone therapy. It's a candid, infuriating, ultimately hopeful conversation about what it will take to close the gender gap in medicine. Hosted on Acast. See acast.com/privacy for more information.
